latin.1850: I. Thesibus superioribus breviter & dilucide, quantum in nobis fuit, exposuimus doctrinam de Libero hominis arbitrio absolute & in se spectato, primo juxta Scholae Reformatae Doctores, deinde juxta mentem Doctorum Scholae Romanae. Ac ante omnia manifestum fecimus nullam esse controversiam de Libero hominis arbitrio circa quaestionem, An sit. Quandoquidem Reformati omnes fatentur non solum hominem, quum primum a Deo conditus est, praeditum fuisse libero arbitrio; sed etiam in homine lapso idem liberum arbitrium mansisse, nec in eo prorsus extinctum & amissum fuisse; quanquam per lapsum hominis valde infirmatum fuerit, & in servitutem peccati redactum, donec per Christi gratiam in libertatem asseratur.
latin.1851: II. Secundo patet ex iis quae ante fuerunt a nobis exposita, utramque scholam in eo convenire quod liberum arbitrium non sit actus, aut habitus aliquis, sed ad facultates animae pertineat: neque tamen sit facultas quaedam reapse ab intellectu & voluntate distincta. Quae autem hodie de liberi arbitrii in homine natura quaestiones moventur alicujus momenti, ad hasce revocari possunt. Cujus facultatis respectu homo dicatur esse liberi Arbitrii? Deinde, Qua in re sita sit libertas a qua liberum in nobis dicitur arbitrium?
latin.1852: III. Quae vero circa quaestiones illas contentio superest, ut ex praecedentibus Thesibus liquere potest, non est proprie inter scholam & scholam; sed inter privatos Doctores qui, in utraque Schola, de hisce rebus varie sentiunt & Philosophantur. Quippe nulla prope sententia in una Schola circa haec obtinet, quae non habeat aliquos in altera Schola patronos. Et nulla saltem ab adversae Scholae Doctoribus rejicitur, quam domestici quoque aliqui non impugnent.
latin.1853: IV. Etenim, ut hinc ordiamur, quum quaeritur ad quam facultatem spectet liberum arbitrium, magna pars Theologorum tum hujus, tum illius Scholae, censet libertatem humani arbitrii a ratione quidem originem quodammodo ducere, & suum habere fundamentum in indeterminatione, sive in αὐτοπραγίᾳ quadam judicii practici; sed tamen illam voluntati soli, tanquam suo subjecto inesse; quod Scholae dicunt libertatem esse in intellectu radicaliter tantum, seu tanquam in causa sine qua non, sed formaliter in sola voluntate. Adeo ut liberum arbitrium non aliud sit quam voluntas, sive simpliciter quatenus rationis judicium & dictamen sequitur, sive quatenus inter plura media a ratione commonstrata unum eligit, alterum repudiat; hoc admittit, vel non admittit.
latin.1854: V. Verum sicut ab ista communiori sententia nonnulli Doctores Reformati recedunt, ita quoque & nuper, & olim, habuit illa in Schola Romana contradictores; olim quidem Durandum, nuper vero Gassendum, ex quorum sententia libertas non est in sola voluntate, sed etiam in intellectu; imo potius & prius in intellectu quam in voluntate. Quanquam fatendum est Doctores Reformatos in hac quaestione liberius versari, & majori cum diversitate sensuum & opinionum; dum alii libertatem ita communem faciunt voluntati & intellectui, ut tamen, juxta hos, ut Josuam Placeum, potiori jure ad voluntatem pertineat, juxta alios vero, ad intellectum, quae est sententia Mosis Amyraldi. Alii vero pertendunt libertatem non esse affectionem hujus aut illius facultatis, sed aliquid ex plurium facultatum concursu, & relatione mutua in homine oriens: adeoque subjectum libertatis proprie non esse hanc, aut illam facultatem, sed simpliciter hominem, quatenus intellectu & voluntate sua certo modo utitur. Ad quam sententiam nos quoque accedimus, quandoquidem homo liber est non simpliciter quatenus vult, nec simpliciter quatenus judicat; sed quatenus ex mentis judicio deliberato, & certo rationis consilio appetit & vult.
latin.1855: VI. Quod spectat autem naturam libertatis, ut clarum etiam est ex iis quae praecedentibus disputationibus exposita fuerunt, non minor est in utraque Schola sententiarum varietas. Et primo quidem abunde probavimus, tam in hac, quam in illa Schola non deesse qui doceant, aliis reclamantibus, libertatem arbitrii oppositam non esse necessitati simpliciter, sed coactioni tantum. Verum illud quoque manifestum fecimus, quae hic est controversia, aut mere verbalem esse, aut saltem non magni momenti. Etenim qui affirmant libertatem in genere opponi non necessitati, sed coactioni solum, diversae sententiae Theologis concedunt, ad libertatem non sufficere immunitatem a coactione; nec libertatem in ea proprie consistere; sed in eo quod agens liberum seipsum movet & seipsum agit, ratione quadam agenti intellectuali propria, quae nec in rebus inanimis, neque in brutis reperitur.
latin.1856: VII. Ac praeterea, quanquam existiment solam coactionem in agente rationali libertati officere, non vero necessitatem, nihilominus agnoscunt agentia libera in plerisque suis actibus, non solum immunia esse a coactione, sed neque esse ad unum necessitate quadam determinata. Adeoque inter actus creaturae liberae, ex eorum sensu nonnulli quidem necessarii sunt, sed plerique tamen contingentes.
latin.1857: VIII. Unde est quod in agentibus liberis triplicem libertatem notant. Prima est quae dicitur in Scholis libertas contrarietatis, sive specificationis, per quam aliquis potest hoc, aut ejus contrarium, vel diversum agere. Secunda est quae dicitur libertas contradictionis, per quam, licet aliquis non possit hoc agere & ejus contrarium, potest tamen agere, & ab actione cessare. Quae utraque libertas opponitur necessitati, & determinationi ad unum, & comitem habet quandam actuum contingentiam. Denique his adjungunt tertiam libertatem, quae vocatur simplex sive complacentiae, per quam agentis liberi voluntas atque intellectus, dum in seipsa reflectuntur, vel tacite, vel expresse, proprios actus probant, & sibi ipsis quodammodo imperant; & ita ratione quadam peculiari seipsa movent, atque agunt; dum, scilicet, intellectus judicat se recte judicare, & sibi judicandum esse prout judicat; voluntas vero vult se velle, & in proprio actu seipsam figit atque firmat. Quae libertas esse potest sine libertate contrarietatis, vel contradictionis, & consistit cum necessaria, atque immutabili determinatione ad unum.
latin.1858: IX. Quum autem libertas extenditur ad actus necessarios atque immutabiles, fatentur illam latiori significatione sumi; libertatem vero strictius acceptam versari tantum circa contingentia, & quae possunt sic, vel secus se habere.
latin.1859: X. Qui vero contra pertendunt, libertatem opponi non coactioni solum, sed etiam necessitati, Theologis diversum sentientibus concedunt voluntatem, seu agens liberum, suorum quorundam actuum ratione habere se necessario; quamvis plerorumque aliorum respectu sese habeat contingenter. Ac praeterea quanquam existiment voluntatem liberam esse respectu tantum eorum actuum qui non necessario, sed contingenter ab ea eliciuntur, nihilominus agnoscunt in illis ipsis actibus ad quos voluntas immutabiliter & necessario determinata est, esse quandam voluntatis libentiam & complacentiam, quae in eo consistit, quod, dum voluntas in suum actum reflectitur, illum probat & sibi imperat, quatenus, scilicet, non vult simpliciter, sed etiam vult se velle, & in proprio actu acquiescit.
latin.1860: [Print dittography, book 422-423: after X the compositor set 'XI. Unde patet, ut dixi, contentionem hic esse verbalem, non realem. Nempe utrique consentiunt quomodo res se in seipsa habeat. Nimirum voluntatem quorundam actuum respectu, habere se necessario; quamvis plerorumque aliorum respectu sese habeat contingenter. Ac praeterea quanquam existiment voluntatem liberam esse respectu tantum eorum actuum qui non necessario, sed contingenter ab ea eliciuntur, nihilominus agnoscunt in illis ipsis actibus ad quos voluntas immutabiliter & necessario determinata est, esse quandam voluntatis libentiam & complacentiam, quae in eo consistit quod dum voluntas in suum actum vel tacite, vel expresse reflectitur, illum probat & sibi imperat, quatenus, scilicet, non vult simpliciter, sed etiam vult se velle, & in proprio actu acquiescit.' and then set XI again in full, as follows.] XI. Unde patet, ut dixi, contentionem hic esse verbalem non realem. Nempe utrique consentiunt quomodo res se in seipsa habeat. Nimirum voluntatem quorundam actuum respectu, habere se necessario, aliorum vero respectu, contingenter. Illam respectu quorundam gaudere libertate contrarietatis, vel contradictionis: sed respectu aliorum esse ad unum determinatam, id est, non posse contrarium agere, vel ab agendo cessare. Et tamen in actibus illis quae necessario elicit voluntas, eam sibi complacere, & suos ipsius actus maxime velle & probare.
latin.1861: XII. Quaestio solum remanet, An actus illi quos voluntas elicit necessario, & inevitabiliter, & respectu quorum prorsus ad unum determinata est, liberi dicendi sint? Negant alii, statuentes eos nullo modo liberos, sed voluntarios solum dicendos esse, quoniam nulla ab ipsis nominatur libertas, quae non sit contrarietatis, vel contradictionis. Alii vero concedunt actus illos liberos quidem non esse, libertate strictius dicta, per quam possumus idem velle & nolle, sive diversum aut contrarium velle, aut saltem velle & non velle, sive a volendo cessare: sed nihilominus pertendunt eosdem actus liberos dici posse & debere libertate latius sumpta, quae est libertas simplex, sive complacentiae. Ita ut quaestio ad istud reducatur; An simplex complacentia, quae voluntati competit respectu omnium suorum actuum, sive necessarii, sive contingentes sint, mereatur, vel non, libertas appellari latiori quadam significatione? quae quaestio ut apparet solum est de nomine.
latin.1862: XIII. Et revera inter eos qui docent libertatem in genere oppositam esse non necessitati sed coactioni, id diserte affirmat Strangius Scholae Reformatae Doctor. Postquam enim multis docuit voluntatem liberam esse non tantum quum versatur circa media, sed etiam quum versatur circa finem, ac proinde Deum libere se amare, & homines libere velle esse foelices, quia libertas voluntatis in genere non est aliud quam spontaneum intellectuale: Et postea fassus est libertatem strictius etiam usurpari, prout versatur circa τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, id est, ea quae sunt in nostra potestate, & restringitur ad media relata ad finem, aut ad ea quae parum, aut nihil ad finem conducunt, quo respectu libertas includit quandam indifferentiam, & actus liberi sunt mere contingentes; Deinde quoque observavit in hoc sensu a multis negari quod Deus libere se amet, & beati in coelo libere Deum diligant, concludit tandem his verbis, Neque nobis videtur hac de re litigandum, quia alioqui tantum esset λογομαχία, non enim negamus, sic vocem liberi arbitrii recte usurpari, quanquam in alio sensu illas actiones diximus esse liberas. De voluntate Dei lib. 3. cap. 14. pag. 687.
latin.1863: XIV. Inter eos vero qui docent libertatem oppositam esse non solum coactioni, sed etiam necessitati, idem agnoscit Guilielmus Estius Scholae Romanae Theologus. Etenim ad loca quaedam Bonaventurae contra sententiam ipsius objecta sic Respondet. Bonaventura quaest. 2. docet liberum arbitrium dupliciter posse considerari: vel ut liberum, vel ut deliberans: Et quidem quatenus liberum est, dicit esse posse respectu necessarii, sicut patet in Deo, & beatis; quia licet in illis habeat necessitatem immutabilitatis, non tamen coactionis. Quatenus autem deliberans, non est, inquit, nisi de contingenti, quia nemo deliberat de necessario & impossibili. Ex qua distinctione satis apparet, quo sensu dixerit liberum arbitrium quatenus liberum est, respicere etiam necessaria, & habere posse actum necessarium. Nam illud quatenus liberum, non aliud est quam quatenus voluntarium & non coactum. Itaque perinde est atque si dicatur, voluntatem quatenus libera est a coactione, versari circa actiones etiam necessarias. Illud vero, quatenus deliberans, id est, ut ipse exponit, quatenus consilians utrum eligat hoc, an illud; intelligitur de libertate quae propria est libero arbitrio ut tali. Igitur Bonaventura non in re discrepat ab aliis, sed minus commode, & praeter communem consuetudinem locutus est.
latin.1864: XV. Neque majoris momenti videtur controversia quae in Schola Reformata manet inter illos ipsos Theologos qui fatentur arbitrii libertatem opponi non coactioni tantum, sed etiam necessitati: dum alii simpliciter docent omnem proprie dictam necessitatem libertati repugnare: alii vero concedunt quidem libertatem oppositam esse naturali necessitati, veruntamen pertendunt multiplicem necessitatem cum eadem arbitrii libertate consistere posse: nimirum agenti libero posse quandam agendi necessitatem imponi per efficaciam gratiae & providentiae divinae, aut etiam per mentis judicium practicum; quae tamen necessitas libertati nihil noceat.
latin.1865: XVI. Etenim qui pertendunt omnem proprie dictam necessitatem cum libertate pugnare, per necessitatem proprie dictam eam duntaxat intelligunt per quam agens, non tantum ad agendum determinatur, sed etiam quae tollit ab eo potestatem non agendi, aut aliter agendi, sive quae constituit agentem in eo statu, ut non solum agat certo & infallibiliter, sed etiam revera non possit non agere; idque non tantum in sensu composito, sed etiam in sensu diviso: ac proinde quae facit ut agens, sive dum agit, sive dum est proxime ad agendum paratus, non habeat talem non agendi, sive aliter agendi potestatem, qualis est in sedente, etiam dum sedet, potestas ambulandi, & vicissim in ambulante sedendi potestas, etiam dum ambulat.
latin.1866: XVII. Itaque concedunt quidem motionem gratiae divinae, & providentiae quoque divinae efficaciam, aut etiam ultimum dictamen judicii practici, sic hominem ad agendum & volendum determinare, ut necessario sequatur actio quae libera dicitur, & impossibile sit ut posita providentiae & gratiae divinae motione & efficacia, non exeratur actus ille ad quem Deus sive per motionem gratiae, sive per providentiae communis efficaciam, hominem praeparat, movet, & determinat. Sed necessitatem istam non habent pro proprie dicta, quoniam cum illa stat vera non agendi potestas. Nempe Deus hominem, quem secundum propositum vocat, sic movet ad credendum Deo, & diligendum Deum & proximum, ut licet infallibiliter inde sequatur fides & dilectio, & posita tali motione, impossibile sit hominem non credere atque diligere, non tamen ab eo tollat potestatem non credendi, & non diligendi, quia cum motione divina non potest quidem compati actus illi contrarius, sed cum ea tamen consistit potestas ad actum contrarium. Non secus ac necesse est sedentem, dum sedet sedere, & ambulantem, dum ambulat, ambulare, & impossibile est ut sedens non sedeat, & ut ambulans non ambulet; & nihilominus manet in sedente vera potestas ambulandi, & in ambulante potestas sedendi; non quidem in sensu composito quasi simul possent ambulare & stare, sed in sensu diviso, quoniam quilibet actus, licet excludat actum oppositum, non tamen excludit potentiam ad illum.
latin.1867: XVIII. Igitur, juxta hanc doctrinam, homo ad hoc vel illud agendum efficaciter a Deo motus, vel judicii proprii dictamine impulsus, necessario quidem agit necessitate quadam infallibilitatis; sed simul tamen veram non agendi potestatem retinet. Et potest quidem non agere, sed certo tamen acturus est: neque contingere potest ut carentia actionis conjungatur unquam cum tali judicio, vel cum ejusmodi Dei motione.
latin.1868: XIX. Qui vero contra docent multiplicem necessitatem cum libertate consistere, & illum quem gratia movet aut judicii proprii dictamen ad agendum impellit, non posse non agere, non aliud sibi volunt quam impossibile esse ut homo qui movetur a Deo ad aliquem actum, gratia illa quae in hominibus operari dicitur velle & perficere, vel saltem providentiae communis efficacia, aut etiam rationis propriae judicio, non eliciat actum illum ad quem sic supponitur motus & excitatus: adeoque ex positione talis gratiae atque auxilii & talis quoque judicii, necessario sequi hominem sic, vel sic acturum.
latin.1869: XX. Caeterum facile concedent, ab eo quem gratia movet, exempli causa, ad orandum, & eleemosynam pauperi largiendam, non omnino propterea tolli potentiam non orandi, & eleemosynam illam non largiendi; imo cum ipso actu invocandi & dandi eleemosynam non minus stare potentiam ad privationem illorum actuum, aut etiam ad actus contrarios, quam cum actu loquendi stat potestas silendi, & cum actu sedendi stat potestas non sedendi, aut etiam ambulandi.
latin.1870: XXI. Utrique ergo in eo conveniunt, necesse esse ut agat ille quem ad agendum movet atque impellit divinae gratiae, vel providentiae vis & efficacia, & rationis propriae dictamen, quoniam ab illa motione Dei & judicii proprii determinatione actio hominis separari non potest: & tamen cum ejusmodi actu, adeoque cum motione Dei ad talem actum consistere potestatem ad cessationem ab illo, aut etiam ad actum oppositum, qua ratione saepius expositum & repetitum est.
latin.1871: XXII. Proinde quum isti quidem asserunt eum quem Deus movet ad actum hunc, aut illum necessario agere; alii vero pertendunt nulla proprie dicta necessitate illum ad agendum impelli, verbis quidem discrepant, idem autem reipsa sentiunt. Nempe priores dicunt ejusmodi hominem necessario agere, quia impossibile est actum ejus a divina motione sejungi, quod alii non negant. Juxta posteriores autem nulla proprie dicta necessitate ad agendum tenetur, quia cum ipso ejus actu, ac proinde multo magis cum motione ad actum, optime consistit potestas ad actum contrarium, vel saltem ad actus istius carentiam, quod priores facile concedent.
latin.1872: XXIII. Indidem quoque apparet facile componi posse dissidium quod adhuc superesse videtur inter Doctores Scholae Reformatae: dum alii, scilicet, affirmant libertatem arbitrii includere quandam agentis liberi indifferentiam, per quam positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, potest agere, vel non agere, hoc aut illud agere; alii vero negant talem indifferentiam libertate includi, aut ad libertatem omnino pertinere.
latin.1873: XXIV. Nam qui volunt libertatem non esse sine aliqua agentis liberi indifferentia, per indifferentiam non intelligunt eum statum in quo agens non inclinat in unam partem magis quam in aliam, sed stat in ancipiti aequali momento huc illuc impellendum quod contrasentientes maxime aversantur. Nec enim ullus est eorum qui tuentur istam indifferentiam, qui non censeat illam in eo quoque reperiri, qui firmo certoque judicio hoc & non aliud sibi agendum esse constituit: & cujus quoque voluntas, habitibus alte radicatis, & quos aegerrime excutere potest, in hanc, aut illam partem vehementissime fertur. Adeoque nomine indifferentiae, in hoc negotio, non aliud designant, quam potentiam veram & intrinsecam non tantum agendi, sed & ab actione cessandi, non tantum hoc agendi, sed & diversum, vel oppositum ejus. Quae potentia non solum in eo reperitur qui dubius & anceps est an agat, vel non agat, sed in eo etiam qui nullo modo haesitat & dubitat de eo quod sibi agendum sive non agendum est, quique proposito fixo, & immoto ad sic & non aliter agendum sese determinat.
latin.1874: XXV. Ac praeterea quum dicunt agens liberum, positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, posse agere vel non agere, hoc, aut illud agere, mens eorum non est quod positis omnibus quae ad aliquem actum voluntatis praerequiruntur, inter quae locum habet gratiae divinae motio, & practicae mentis judicium, possit actio voluntatis non sequi, & sic carentia actionis ejus jungi cum omnibus illis per quae voluntas ad agendum movetur atque disponitur. Fatentur enim impossibile esse ut Deus hominem quempiam gratia sua efficaci ad aliquem actum pietatis moveat, & tamen actus ille ab eo non eliciatur: aut ut aliquis, omnibus expensis, judicet hic & nunc istud sibi agendum & appetendum esse, & tamen idem istud non agat & appetat; Verum id solum sibi volunt illum qui, qua jam dictum est ratione, ad agendum movetur, licet infallibiliter & certo acturus sit, & contingere non possit ut non agat; illum, inquam, nihilominus veram in se retinere potentiam non agendi, & aliter agendi, quae manet non solum in eo qui proxime ad agendum paratus & dispositus est, sed in eo ipso qui jam de facto agit; quoniam etsi cum actu aliquo stare non possit ejus carentia, aut actus contrarius, optime tamen cum eo componi potest potentia ad actum illum contrarium, ut jam pluries inculcatum fuit.
latin.1875: XXVI. Qui vero contra pugnant ad libertatem arbitrii non requiri aliquam agentis indifferentiam, indifferentiae nomine significare videntur voluntatis ἰσοῤῥοπίαν, quum in hanc partem non magis quam in aliam propendet, & huc non magis quam illuc flexilis est, qua in re nullus eorum qui in Scholis Christianis Theologi nomen ferunt, libertatem unquam constituit.
latin.1876: XXVII. Et similiter quum dicunt falsum esse quod agens liberum, positis omnibus quae sunt ad agendum requisita, possit agere, & non agere, hoc & illud agere, sententia eorum non est, per ea quae ad agendum praeparant & impellunt, ab agente libero tolli facultatem aliter agendi, aut actionem suspendendi: quandoquidem agnoscunt facultatem illam per actum ipsum non tolli; nedum per ea quae ad agendum impellunt. Nec enim negant eum qui per Dei gratiam egentis miseretur, in se semper habere potestatem non miserendi, & qui mundi hujus voluptates contemnit, retinere facultatem illas quaerendi atque amplectendi, quae per divinam gratiam ab eo non aufertur. Adeoque non aliud intendunt quam hoc, positis omnibus quae requiruntur ad agendum, contingere non posse ut agens liberum non agat: licet alioqui maneat in eo facultas qua posset non agere, aut aliter agere. Exempli gratia, fieri non posse quin positis omnibus quae ex parte Dei necessaria sunt ad fidem & conversionem hominis producendam, homo convertatur & credat; quanquam semper, & etiam quum credit & convertitur, in eo maneat facultas, qua non credere & non converti posset.
latin.1877: XXVIII. Unde patet hos Theologos, quum negant libertatem consistere in quadam agentis indifferentia, duo tantum ob oculos habere, quorum unum est libertatem non consistere in ejus qui liber dicitur ancipiti statu, in quo non magis inclinat & propendet ad agendum, quam ad non agendum: alterum, posita gratiae & providentiae divinae motione & efficacia, & etiam proprii judicii dictamine, contingere non posse ut agens liberum non agat id ad quod, tum efficaci illa motione Dei, tum judicio proprio, impellitur; quod utrumque ultro fatentur illi ex Reformatis qui docent arbitrii libertate includi quandam ad agendum indifferentiam. Et Rursus ex dictis non minus evidens est Doctores illos qui tuentur istam indifferentiam hoc solum in animo habere quod divina motio, & practicae mentis judicium sic hominem ad agendum movent, ut ex una parte quidem certo & infallibiliter agat, ex altera tamen non tollatur ab eo facultas non agendi, aut aliter agendi. Non secus ac quum homo reipsa agit, eadem facultas non tollitur ab eo per actum ipsum ad quem motus & impulsus est.
latin.1878: XXIX. Ex omnibus autem hisce manifestum est Reformatorum hac in parte doctrinam recte expositam atque intellectam, & ex mente eorum a quibus proponitur, reipsa non differre a sententia eorum qui in Schola Romana receptiores Thomistae appellantur. Quamvis enim contendant libertatem opponi non coactioni solum, sed necessitati quoque naturali & proprie dictae, nihilominus agnoscunt positis omnibus quae sunt ad agendum praerequisita, necessario sequi actum creaturae liberae necessitate quadam infallibilitatis. Quia licet agens liberum semper in se retineat potestatem non agendi, etiam quum reipsa agit, & a fortiori quum est in proximo ad agendum; positis tamen omnibus quae, tum ex parte Dei, tum ex parte intellectus praerequiruntur ut voluntas agat, agit illa certo & infallibiliter, & impossibile est actionem ejus non sequi. Nempe ex eorum doctrina, cum omnibus illis quae sunt ad agendum praerequisita optime conjungi & consistere potest potentia non agendi, aut aliter agendi, non tamen carentia actus, & multo minus actus contrarius.
latin.1879: XXX. Adeoque per indifferentiam ad agendum, vel non agendum, in qua ex eorum mente libertas constituenda est, aut quae saltem libertati est necessario juncta, non aliam intelligunt, quam quae supra jam descripta fuit. Nimirum neque talem per quam causa libera concipiatur dubia & anceps an agat, vel non agat; neque etiam per quam positis omnibus quae sunt ad agendum requisita, contingere possit ut agens liberum tam non agat, quam agat; sed quae non aliud sit quam vera non agendi, & aliter agendi potestas, quae manet in causa libera quum positis omnibus quae ad agendum requiruntur, non solum est in proximo ut agat, sed etiam infallibiliter & certo actura est, prout Alvarez suam hac de re sententiam clare admodum & diserte exponit in summa operis de auxiliis divinae gratiae lib. 4. cap. 14. unde desumpta sunt verba quae ex eodem Alvarez superiori disputatione a nobis relata sunt.
latin.1880: XXXI. Ac profecto eandem plane hic esse sententiam Didaci istius Alvares, & aliorum qui cum eo recentiores Thomistae nuncupantur, cum sententia Doctorum Ecclesiae Reformatae, testis idoneus est Vir Doctissimus Andreas Rivetus ante annos aliquot in Academia Leydensi Professor, dum non aliis verbis quam quae sunt ex ipso Alvarez desumpta, mentem suam de arbitrii humani libertate exprimere voluit. In summa controversiarum tract. 4. quaest. 3. Fatetur enim tolerari posse definitionem liberi arbitrii per quam dicitur facultas voluntatis qua, positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, possit agere, aut non agere, dummodo id intelligatur non in sensu composito, sed in sensu diviso, Nempe, inquit, si quis dicat positis omnibus antecedenter requisitis, secundum ordinem rationis, vel temporis ad actum, liberum arbitrium posse operari, vel non operari, ita videlicet, ut cum eisdem praerequisitis stet simul in libero arbitrio facultas & potentia, qua possit operari, vel non operari si vellet, ut distinguit Didacus Alvares, quia etiam motio Dei efficax qua ad talem actum voluntas determinatur, non tollit a libero arbitrio facultatem operandi illum actum vel operandi actum contrarium, sed solum efficit, quod cum liberum arbitrium possit operari vel non operari talem actum infallibiliter, libere tamen operetur illum. Quod cum facit, manet potentia ad alium, quia ad tales actus non est naturaliter determinata. Nam ut ait idem, in causa contingenti & libera, simul est potentia ad utrumque oppositum, non tamen est potentia ad opposita simul habenda, quia potentia ad actum unum, non repugnat potentiae ad actum contrarium, nec etiam repugnat actui contrario, actus autem contrarii repugnant inter se in eodem subjecto; unde liberum arbitrium creatum non solum antequam determinetur ad unum actum, sed etiam in ipso instanti, in quo determinatur a Deo, & seipsum determinat ad eundem actum, simul habet potentiam qua potest actum contrarium producere si velit, non tamen ad actum contrarium simul habendum, quia duo actus contrarii simul in eadem potentia esse non possunt, sed successive. Quae omnia verba ex Didaco Alvarez vel expresse citata, vel saltem mutuata sunt, ut & illud quod subjungit tanquam ejusdem doctoris conclusionem quae ipsi probatur, nempe, non esse de ratione liberi arbitrii aut definitione ejus, quod positis omnibus secundum ordinem causalitatis antecedenter praerequisitis ad operandum talem actum, possit eundem actum non operari in sensu composito, si compositio fiat inter hujusmodi praerequisita, & carentiam talis actus, seu actum contrarium, id est, cum auxilio Dei efficaci, non simul stare quod liberum arbitrium non producat actum dilectionis, aut eliciat actum dilectioni Dei contrarium.
latin.1881: XXXII. Nulla ergo Reformatis controversia superest, quae realis sit & alicujus momenti, nisi cum iis qui in Schola Romana Molinistae dicuntur, denominatione sumpta a Ludovico Molina Jesuita celeberrimo, qui ante annos centum circiter scripsit & docuit. Quippe indifferentiam ad agendum & non agendum, in qua libertas arbitrii consistit, & vulgatam definitionem per quam dicitur esse id quo, positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, potest voluntas agere & non agere, hoc aut illud agere, longe aliter intelligunt quam Thomistae recentiores, ut praecedenti disputatione manifestum fecimus.

Fatentur quidem cum aliis per indifferentiam de qua hic quaestio est, non significari eam voluntatis constitutionem per quam non magis huc propendeat quam illuc, sed inter duo opposita haereat, quasi suspensa in aequilibrio: cum agnoscant libertati nihil praejudicari per habitus quibus voluntas ad hoc potius quam illud agendum fortiter inclinatur, & difficulter alio ferri potest. Et praeterea non negant in sensu quodam composito falsum esse quod voluntas possit agere & non agere, hoc & illud agere; nempe, si quis per hoc significari putet actum & ejus carentiam, aut duos actus contrarios in voluntate simul stare & componi posse. Admittunt quoque per indifferentiam in qua libertatis essentia consistit, non intelligi potestatem bene vel male agendi. Agnoscunt enim libertatem arbitrii manere etiam in eo qui non potest bene agere, ut in spiritibus damnatis: & multo magis adhuc illam in eo reperiri qui male agere non potest, ut in sanctis qui faciem Dei vident, & cum eo in coelo regnant.
latin.1883: XXXIV. Sed acriter defendunt voluntatem in se sic indeterminatam & indifferentem esse, ut positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis, sive ex parte Dei, sive ex parte objecti, sive ex parte intellectus, fieri possit & saepe etiam eveniat, ut voluntas non agat: adeoque nihil esse eorum quae voluntatem antecedenter ad agendum movent atque incitant, quo posito non possit voluntatis actio non sequi, & saepius etiam reapse non sequatur: & sic cum omnibus illis quae actionem voluntatis praecedunt, & ad eam praerequiruntur, revera conjungi & componi posse, non solum potestatem ad non agendum aut aliud agendum, sed ipsam actus carentiam, & actum quoque contrarium. Quod negant, ut satis liquet ex antedictis, non solum Reformati, verum etiam Thomistae illi recentiores. Quippe sentiunt cum iis quae vel ex parte Dei, vel ex parte intellectus ad agendum necessaria sunt, posse quidem in voluntate consistere potestatem non agendi, vel agendi oppositum; sed tamen iis positis voluntatem semper agere, nec fieri posse ut aliter eveniat: quoniam ex hac hypothesi voluntas agit certo & infallibiliter, licet in se retineat non agendi potentiam.
latin.1884: XXXV. Porro cum lis ista apud Romanos Pontifices, & coetum Cardinalium ad hoc deputatorum saepe fuerit mota & agitata, hactenus tamen illam nondum definierunt, & licitum suis esse voluerunt hanc aut illam sententiam pro arbitrio tenere & tueri. Quanquam sicut sub hujus saeculi initium & praecedentis finem Thomistarum sententiae favere visi sunt Romani Pontifices Paulus V. & Clemens VIII. latin.1885: XXXVI. Ac praeterea sicut hac in parte communibus armis Molinistas impugnant cum Reformatis illis qui Dordracenae Synodo subscribunt, nonnulli Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, ut qui vocantur Jansenistae, & Thomistae illi quoque recentiores: sic a parte Molinistarum stant, & eorum in hac quaestione doctrinam acerrime defendunt illi ex Reformatis qui in Belgio dicuntur Remonstrantes sive Arminiani, aliique qui Dordracenam Synodum non sequuntur.

Eorum autem sententia hoc praecipue nomine a Scholae Reformatae Doctoribus rejicitur quod divinae gratiae efficaciam minuit, & libero arbitrio plus tribuit quam par est in salutis negotio. latin.1887: XXXVIII. Praeterea scriptura docet gratiam divinam esse quae discrimen inter homines ponit, inter eos scilicet qui convertuntur & qui non convertuntur, inter credentes atque incredulos inter eos qui Deo vocanti parent & eos qui illi resistunt: secundum illud Pauli, Quis te discernit? sed ex doctrina eorum de quibus jam agimus, sequitur non gratiam divinam; sed simpliciter voluntatem humanam hoc discrimen inter homines constituere. Supponit enim aequali gratia pluribus oblata, hunc credere; illum non credere; hunc converti, illum non converti: Et consequenter quod hic potius quam ille credit & convertitur, ad aliquam gratiae efficaciam referri non debere, sed solum ad liberam voluntatis humanae determinationem; quia nimirum hic gratiae moventi & praevenienti consentire voluit, ille vero noluit.
latin.1888: XXXIX. Adde quod si gratia divina sic tantum homines movet, praeparat & incitat ad volendum & perficiendum ea quae Deus jubet, ut tamen ipsum velle & perficere, ea posita, possit in homine non sequi, & de facto saepe non sequatur, operatur illa quidem in homine vires seu dispositiones necessarias ad bonum volendum & perficiendum, non autem ipsum velle & perficere. latin.1889: XL. Nolite, inquit, murmurare inter vos. Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater qui misit me traxerit eum. Est scriptum in Prophetis, Et erunt omnes docti a Deo. Cum ergo sit quaedam divina gratia, & quidem electis omnibus communis, ad cujus motionem atque impulsionem hominis conversio infallibiliter & certo consequitur; & tamen omnium consensu conversio hominis ad Deum sit liber voluntatis actus: planum est libertatem in eo male constitui, quod positis omnibus ad agendum praerequisitis ipsaque ordinaria gratiae motione, voluntas semper possit tam non agere quam agere, non tantum in sensu diviso sed in sensu quoque composito, ita ut cum illa gratiae motione conjungi possit carentia actus ad quem hominem movet.

Aut etiam illa Bellarmini, Liberum arbitrium est libera potestas ex his quae ad finem aliquem conducunt unum prae alio eligendi, aut unum & idem respuendi vel acceptandi pro arbitrio nostro, ad magnam Dei gloriam attributa vel concessa.

sections.title: No controversy over whether free choice exists: the Reformed hold it survives the fall, weakened and enslaved
sections.pass_a: In the preceding Theses we have set forth briefly and clearly, as far as lay in us, the doctrine of the free choice of man considered absolutely and in itself, first according to the Doctors of the Reformed School, then according to the mind of the Doctors of the Roman School. And before all things we made it manifest that there is no controversy about the free choice of man concerning the question, Whether it be. Since all the Reformed confess not only that man, when he was first created by God, was endowed with free choice; but also that in fallen man the same free choice has remained, and has not been altogether extinguished and lost in him; although through man's fall it has been greatly weakened, and reduced into the bondage of sin, until it be set into liberty through the grace of Christ.
pass_b: The foregoing theses have set out, as briefly and clearly as we could, the doctrine of man's free choice taken absolutely and in itself: first as the teachers of the Reformed School hold it, then as the teachers of the Roman School understand it.

Above all, they showed that there is no dispute over whether man has free choice at all. Every Reformed theologian grants that man was given free choice when God first made him, and that the same free choice survived in man after the fall and was not wholly destroyed or lost. The fall badly weakened it and brought it into slavery to sin, until Christ's grace sets it free.

sections.title: Both Schools agree free choice is a faculty, not really distinct from intellect and will; two questions remain
sections.pass_a: Secondly it is plain from those things which were before set forth by us, that both schools agree in this, that free choice is not an act, or any habit, but pertains to the faculties of the soul: and yet that it is not some faculty really distinct from the intellect and will. But the questions of any moment which are moved today concerning the nature of free choice in man may be brought back to these. In respect of what faculty is man said to be of free Choice? Next, In what thing is that liberty placed from which choice is called free in us?
pass_b: Second, what we set out earlier makes it clear that both schools agree that free choice is neither an act nor a habit but belongs among the soul's faculties, and yet is not a faculty really distinct from intellect and will.

The questions of any weight now raised about the nature of man's free choice come down to two. With respect to which faculty is man said to have free choice? And what does the freedom consist in, on account of which our choice is called free?

sections.title: The remaining dispute lies between individual doctors, not between the Schools
sections.pass_a: But the contention which remains about those questions, as may be clear from the preceding Theses, is not properly between school and school; but between private Doctors who, in either School, think and Philosophize variously about these things. Indeed almost no opinion obtains in one School about these matters, which has not some patrons in the other School. And at least none is rejected by the Doctors of the opposite School, which some of its own also do not attack.
pass_b: As the earlier theses show, whatever dispute remains on those questions is not really between one school and the other. It is between individual teachers who, in both schools, think and reason about these matters in different ways.

Hardly any view on them prevails in one school without having some defenders in the other. And at least no view is rejected by teachers of the opposing school without being attacked as well by some teachers of its own school.

sections.title: The common view in both Schools: freedom rooted in the intellect, formally in the will alone
sections.pass_a: For, to begin from here, when it is asked to what faculty free choice belongs, a great part of the Theologians both of this and of that School judges that the liberty of human choice indeed in a manner draws its origin from reason, and has its foundation in the indetermination, or in a certain self-action (αὐτοπραγία) of the practical judgment; but yet that it inheres in the will alone, as in its subject; which the Schools express by saying that liberty is in the intellect only radically, or as in a cause without which not, but formally in the will alone. So that free choice is nothing else than the will, either simply in so far as it follows the judgment and dictate of reason, or in so far as among several means shown by reason it chooses one, rejects another; admits this, or does not admit it.
pass_b: To start here: when people ask which faculty free choice belongs to, a large share of the theologians of both schools hold that the freedom of human choice does in some way take its origin from reason and rests on the practical judgment's indetermination, or on a kind of self-action (αὐτοπραγία) in it, yet resides in the will alone as its subject.

The Schools put it this way: freedom is in the intellect only as its root, or as a cause without which it could not be, but it is formally in the will alone. On that view free choice is simply the will, whether insofar as it follows reason's judgment and dictate, or insofar as, among several means that reason points out, it takes one and refuses another, accepting this or not accepting it.

sections.title: Dissent: Durandus and Gassendi; Placaeus and Amyraut; Le Blanc's view that the subject of freedom is the man
sections.pass_a: But as some Reformed Doctors depart from that more common opinion, so also both lately and of old it has had opponents in the Roman School; of old indeed Durandus, but lately Gassendi, in whose opinion liberty is not in the will alone, but also in the intellect; nay rather and earlier in the intellect than in the will. Although it must be confessed that the Reformed Doctors move more freely in this question, and with greater diversity of senses and opinions; while some make liberty so common to will and intellect, that yet, according to these, as Joshua Placaeus, it belongs by the better right to the will, but according to others, to the intellect, which is the opinion of Moses Amyraldus. But others contend that liberty is not an affection of this or that faculty, but something arising in man from the concurrence of several faculties, and their mutual relation: and so that the subject of liberty properly is not this, or that faculty, but simply man, in so far as he uses his intellect and will in a certain manner. To which opinion we also accede, since man is free not simply in so far as he wills, nor simply in so far as he judges; but in so far as he desires and wills from the deliberate judgment of the mind, and by the certain counsel of reason.
pass_b: Just as some Reformed teachers depart from that more common view, it has also had critics in the Roman School, both long ago and recently: Durandus in the past and Gassendi now. In their view freedom is not in the will alone but in the intellect as well, and indeed more, and first, in the intellect than in the will.

Admittedly the Reformed teachers handle this question more freely, and their senses and opinions vary more widely. Some make freedom common to will and intellect, yet hold that it belongs with the stronger claim to the will, as Josué de la Place (Placaeus) does, while others give that claim to the intellect, which is the view of Moïse Amyraut.

Others insist that freedom is not a property of one faculty or another but something that arises in man from several faculties working together and bearing on one another. Its proper subject is then neither this faculty nor that but simply the man, insofar as he uses his intellect and will in a certain way. We take this view too, since a man is free not simply insofar as he wills, nor simply insofar as he judges, but insofar as he desires and wills on the basis of his mind's deliberate judgment and a settled counsel of reason.

sections.title: On the nature of freedom: whether it opposes necessity or only compulsion is a verbal or minor dispute
sections.pass_a: But as regards the nature of liberty, as is also clear from those things which were set forth in the preceding disputations, there is no less variety of opinions in either School. And first indeed we have abundantly proved, that both in this, and in that School there are not wanting those who teach, others protesting, that liberty of choice is opposed not to necessity simply, but to compulsion only. But we made this also manifest, that the controversy which is here, is either merely verbal, or at least not of great moment. For those who affirm that liberty in general is opposed not to necessity, but to compulsion only, grant to the Theologians of a different opinion, that immunity from compulsion does not suffice for liberty; nor does liberty properly consist in it; but in this, that a free agent moves itself and acts itself, by a certain manner proper to an intellectual agent, which is found neither in inanimate things, nor in brutes.
pass_b: On the nature of freedom, as the earlier disputations also make clear, opinion varies no less in both schools. First, we showed at length that in each school some teach, against the protests of others, that freedom of choice is opposed not to necessity as such but only to compulsion.

We also showed that the dispute here is either a mere matter of words or at least of little weight. Those who say that freedom in general is opposed only to compulsion, not to necessity, concede to theologians of the other view that being free from compulsion is not enough for freedom and is not, properly, what freedom consists in. It consists rather in the free agent's moving and acting itself, in a way peculiar to an intelligent agent and found neither in lifeless things nor in animals.

sections.title: They also grant that most free acts are not fixed on one course but contingent
sections.pass_a: And moreover, although they think that compulsion alone in a rational agent hinders liberty, not necessity, nevertheless they acknowledge that free agents in most of their acts, are not only immune from compulsion, but are not determined to one by a certain necessity either. And so among the acts of a free creature, in their sense, some indeed are necessary, but most yet contingent.
pass_b: Besides, although they think that in a rational agent only compulsion stands in the way of freedom, and necessity does not, they still recognize that in most of their acts free agents are not only free from compulsion but are also not fixed on one course by any necessity.
So, on their account, some of a free creature's acts are necessary, but most are contingent.

sections.title: Three freedoms: of contrariety or specification, of contradiction, and simple freedom or complacency
sections.pass_a: Whence it is that in free agents they note a threefold liberty. The first is that which is called in the Schools liberty of contrariety, or of specification, by which one can do this, or its contrary, or something different. The second is that which is called liberty of contradiction, by which, although one cannot do this and its contrary, yet he can act, and cease from action. Both which liberties are opposed to necessity, and to determination to one, and have as companion a certain contingency of acts. Lastly to these they join a third liberty, which is called simple or of complacency, by which the will and intellect of a free agent, while they are reflected upon themselves, either tacitly, or expressly, approve their own acts, and in a manner command themselves; and so by a certain peculiar manner move and act themselves; while, namely, the intellect judges that it judges rightly, and that it must judge as it judges; but the will wills that it wills, and fixes and confirms itself in its own act. Which liberty can be without liberty of contrariety, or of contradiction, and consists with a necessary, and immutable determination to one.
pass_b: They therefore distinguish three kinds of freedom in free agents. The first, called in the Schools freedom of contrariety or of specification, is the power to do this, or its contrary, or something else.

The second, called freedom of contradiction, is the power, even where one cannot do this and its contrary, at least to act or to stop acting. Both of these are opposed to necessity and to being fixed on one course, and both go together with a certain contingency in one's acts.

To these they add a third, called simple freedom or freedom of complacency. Here a free agent's will and intellect turn back on themselves, tacitly or explicitly, approve their own acts, and in a way give orders to themselves, and so move and act themselves in a manner all their own: the intellect judges that it is judging rightly and that it ought to judge as it does, and the will wills its own willing and fixes and settles itself in its own act. This freedom can exist without freedom of contrariety or of contradiction, and it is compatible with a necessary and unchangeable determination to one course.

sections.title: Freedom extended to necessary acts is taken in a broader sense
sections.pass_a: But when liberty is extended to necessary and immutable acts, they confess that it is taken in a wider signification; but that liberty more strictly accepted is concerned only with contingent things, and those which can be so, or otherwise.
pass_b: They admit that when freedom is stretched to cover acts that are necessary and unchangeable, the word is being used in a broader sense.
Taken more strictly, freedom deals only with what is contingent: with what may turn out one way or the other.

sections.title: Those who oppose freedom to necessity grant some necessary acts and a willingness or complacency in them
sections.pass_a: But those who on the contrary contend, that liberty is opposed not to compulsion only, but also to necessity, grant to the Theologians who think differently that the will, or free agent, holds itself necessarily in respect of certain of its acts; although in respect of most others it holds itself contingently. And moreover although they judge the will to be free in respect only of those acts which are elicited by it not necessarily, but contingently, nevertheless they acknowledge in those very acts to which the will is immutably & necessarily determined, that there is a certain willingness and complacency of the will, which consists in this, that, while the will is reflected upon its own act, it approves it and commands itself, in so far, namely, as it does not will simply, but also wills that it wills, and rests in its own act.
pass_b: Those who hold the opposite, that freedom is opposed not only to compulsion but to necessity as well, concede to the theologians who disagree that the will, or free agent, stands necessarily toward some of its acts, though it stands contingently toward most of the others.

They also think the will is free only with respect to the acts it produces contingently rather than necessarily. Yet they recognize that even in the acts on which the will is fixed unchangeably and necessarily there is a certain willingness and complacency of the will. When the will turns back on its act it approves it and gives itself the order, since it does not simply will but also wills its own willing and rests content in its act.

sections.title: Hence the contention is verbal: both agree on how the matter stands
sections.pass_a: [Print dittography, book 422-423: after X the compositor set 'XI. Hence it appears, as I said, that the contention here is verbal, not real. Namely both agree how the thing stands in itself. To wit, that the will in respect of certain acts holds itself necessarily; although in respect of most others it holds itself contingently. And moreover although they judge the will to be free in respect only of those acts which are elicited by it not necessarily, but contingently, nevertheless they acknowledge in those very acts to which the will is immutably and necessarily determined, that there is a certain willingness and complacency of the will, which consists in this, that while the will is reflected upon its own act either tacitly, or expressly, it approves it and commands itself, in so far, namely, as it does not will simply, but also wills that it wills, and rests in its own act.' and then set XI again in full, as follows.] XI. Hence it appears, as I said, that the contention here is verbal not real. Namely both agree how the thing stands in itself. To wit, that the will in respect of certain acts holds itself necessarily, but in respect of others, contingently. That in respect of certain ones it enjoys liberty of contrariety, or of contradiction: but in respect of others is determined to one, that is, cannot do the contrary, or cease from acting. And yet in those acts which the will elicits necessarily, that it is pleased with itself, and most of all wills and approves its own acts.
pass_b: [The 1675 print sets this thesis twice. The first setting joins the opening words below to a repeat of the second half of X, adding only 'tacitly or explicitly'; the full thesis follows.]

This shows, as I said, that the dispute here is about words, not substance. Both sides agree on how the matter actually stands: the will stands necessarily toward some acts and contingently toward others. Toward some it enjoys freedom of contrariety or contradiction, while toward others it is fixed on one course, that is, it cannot do the opposite or stop acting.
And yet in the acts it produces necessarily, the will is pleased with itself and supremely wills and approves its own acts.

sections.title: The only remaining question, whether necessary acts should be called free, concerns a name
sections.pass_a: The question only remains, Whether those acts which the will elicits necessarily, and inevitably, and in respect of which it is altogether determined to one, are to be called free? Some deny it, laying down that they are in no way free, but are to be called voluntary only, since no liberty is named by them which is not of contrariety, or of contradiction. But others grant that those acts indeed are not free, by liberty more strictly so called, by which we can will and refuse the same thing, or will something different or contrary, or at least will and not will, or cease from willing: but nevertheless they contend that the same acts can and ought to be called free by liberty more largely taken, which is simple liberty, or of complacency. So that the question is reduced to this; Whether the simple complacency, which belongs to the will in respect of all its acts, whether they be necessary, or contingent, deserves, or not, to be called liberty in a certain wider signification? which question as appears is only about the name.
pass_b: Only one question remains: should the acts the will produces necessarily and inevitably, toward which it is entirely fixed on one course, be called free? Some say no. They hold that such acts are in no way free and should be called only voluntary, because the only freedom they recognize is that of contrariety or of contradiction.

Others grant that these acts are not free in the stricter sense of freedom, the sense in which we can will and refuse the same thing, or will something different or contrary, or at least will or not will, that is, stop willing. But they insist that the same acts can and should be called free in a broader sense, namely simple freedom, or freedom of complacency.

The question therefore comes down to this: does the simple complacency that belongs to the will in all its acts, necessary and contingent alike, deserve to be called freedom in some broader sense or not? Plainly that is a question about a name only.

sections.title: Strang concedes it would be a mere war of words (De voluntate Dei III.14, p. 687)
sections.pass_a: And indeed among those who teach that liberty in general is opposed not to necessity but to compulsion, Strang a Doctor of the Reformed School expressly affirms this. For after he had taught at length that the will is free not only when it is concerned with means, but also when it is concerned with the end, and accordingly that God loves himself freely, and men freely will to be happy, because the liberty of the will in general is nothing else than the intellectual spontaneous: And afterwards had confessed that liberty is used also more strictly, as it is concerned with τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, that is, those things which are in our power, and is restricted to means related to the end, or to those which conduce little, or nothing to the end, in which respect liberty includes a certain indifference, and free acts are merely contingent; Then also had observed that in this sense it is denied by many that God freely loves himself, and that the blessed in heaven freely love God, he concludes at length in these words, Nor does it seem to us that we must contend about this matter, because otherwise it would be only a logomachy, for we do not deny, that the word free choice is rightly used thus, although in another sense we have said those actions are free. On the will of God book 3. chap. 14. page 687.
pass_b: Among those who teach that freedom in general is opposed not to necessity but to compulsion, the Reformed teacher John Strang says this in so many words. He first argued at length that the will is free not only in dealing with means but also in dealing with the end, so that God loves himself freely and men freely will to be happy, since freedom of the will in general is nothing but intellectual spontaneity.

He then admitted that freedom is also used in a narrower sense, for what concerns τὰ ἐφ' ἡμῖν, the things in our power, and limited to means ordered to the end, or to things that contribute little or nothing to the end. In that respect freedom includes a certain indifference, and free acts are purely contingent. He further noted that many deny, in this sense, that God loves himself freely or that the blessed in heaven love God freely.

He finally concludes: 'We do not think this matter worth a quarrel, since it would otherwise be a mere war of words (λογομαχία). For we do not deny that the term free choice is properly used in that way, although in another sense we have called those actions free.' (De voluntate Dei, book 3, chapter 14, page 687.)

sections.title: Estius on Bonaventure: free choice as free and as deliberating; Bonaventure differs only in wording
sections.pass_a: But among those who teach that liberty is opposed not only to compulsion, but also to necessity, William Estius a Theologian of the Roman School acknowledges the same. For to certain places of Bonaventure objected against his own opinion he Answers thus. Bonaventure in question 2. teaches that free choice can be considered in two ways: either as free, or as deliberating: And indeed in so far as it is free, he says it can be in respect of the necessary, as appears in God, and the blessed; because although in them it has a necessity of immutability, yet not of compulsion. But in so far as deliberating, it is not, he says, except of the contingent, because no one deliberates of the necessary and impossible. From which distinction it appears sufficiently, in what sense he said that free choice in so far as it is free, regards also necessary things, and can have a necessary act. For that 'in so far as free', is nothing else than in so far as voluntary and not compelled. Therefore it is just as if it were said, that the will in so far as it is free from compulsion, is concerned about actions even necessary. But that 'in so far as deliberating', that is, as he himself explains, in so far as taking counsel whether it should choose this, or that; is understood of the liberty which is proper to free choice as such. Therefore Bonaventure does not differ in substance from others, but spoke less fitly, and beside the common custom.
pass_b: Among those who teach that freedom is opposed not only to compulsion but also to necessity, the Roman theologian William Estius grants the same point. Replying to passages of Bonaventure brought against his own view, he says:

'In question 2 Bonaventure teaches that free choice can be considered in two ways, as free or as deliberating. As free, he says, it can bear on what is necessary, as is plain in God and the blessed, for although in them it has a necessity of unchangeableness, it has none of compulsion. As deliberating, he says, it concerns only the contingent, since no one deliberates about what is necessary or impossible.

This distinction shows well enough in what sense he said that free choice, as free, also looks to necessary things and can have a necessary act. For "as free" means nothing other than "as voluntary and not compelled". It is as if he said that the will, insofar as it is free from compulsion, deals even with necessary actions.

"As deliberating", on the other hand, meaning, as he explains, as weighing whether to choose this or that, refers to the freedom that belongs to free choice as such. Bonaventure therefore does not disagree with the others in substance; he merely spoke less aptly and against common usage.'

sections.title: Within the Reformed School: whether every necessity properly so called conflicts with freedom
sections.pass_a: Nor does the controversy seem of greater moment which remains in the Reformed School among those very Theologians who confess that liberty of choice is opposed not to compulsion only, but also to necessity: while some simply teach that all necessity properly so called is repugnant to liberty: but others grant indeed that liberty is opposed to natural necessity, yet contend that manifold necessity can consist with the same liberty of choice: namely that a certain necessity of acting can be imposed on a free agent through the efficacy of divine grace and providence, or also through the practical judgment of the mind; which necessity yet does no harm to liberty.
pass_b: The dispute that remains within the Reformed School, among the very theologians who admit that freedom of choice is opposed not only to compulsion but also to necessity, seems no weightier.

Some of them teach without qualification that every necessity in the proper sense conflicts with freedom. Others grant that freedom is opposed to natural necessity but insist that necessity of many kinds can coexist with that same freedom of choice. A free agent, they say, can have a certain necessity of acting laid on it by the efficacy of God's grace and providence, or even by the mind's practical judgment, and that necessity does freedom no harm.

sections.title: What the first party means by necessity properly so called: removal of the power to act otherwise
sections.pass_a: For those who contend that all necessity properly so called conflicts with liberty, by necessity properly so called understand only that by which an agent, is not only determined to acting, but also which takes from him the power of not acting, or of acting otherwise, or which places the agent in that state, that he not only acts certainly and infallibly, but also really cannot not act; and that not only in the composed sense, but also in the divided sense: and accordingly which makes that the agent, whether while he acts, or while he is proximately prepared to act, has not such a power of not acting, or of acting otherwise, as is in one sitting, even while he sits, the power of walking, and in turn in one walking the power of sitting, even while he walks.
pass_b: Those who insist that every necessity properly so called conflicts with freedom mean by that phrase only a necessity that does more than determine the agent to act. It also removes his power not to act or to act otherwise; it puts him in a condition where he not only acts surely and infallibly but really cannot fail to act, and that not only in the composite sense but in the divided sense too.

Such a necessity would leave the agent, whether he is acting or is on the point of acting, without the kind of power not to act, or to act otherwise, that a seated man has to walk even while he sits, and a walking man has to sit even while he walks.

sections.title: Grace, providence and the last practical dictate determine infallibly, yet the power not to act remains
sections.pass_a: Therefore they grant indeed that the motion of divine grace, and the efficacy also of divine providence, or even the last dictate of the practical judgment, so determine man to acting and willing, that the action which is called free necessarily follows, and it is impossible that, the motion and efficacy of providence and divine grace being posited, that act should not be put forth to which God whether through the motion of grace, or through the efficacy of common providence, prepares, moves, and determines man. But they do not hold that necessity for necessity properly so called, since with it stands a true power of not acting. Namely God so moves man, whom he calls according to his purpose, to believing God, and loving God and neighbour, that although faith and love infallibly follow thence, and, such a motion being posited, it is impossible that the man should not believe and love, yet he does not take from him the power of not believing, and not loving, because with the divine motion the act contrary to it indeed cannot be compatible, but with it yet consists the power to the contrary act. Not otherwise than it is necessary that one sitting, while he sits, sit, and one walking, while he walks, walk, and it is impossible that one sitting should not sit, and that one walking should not walk; and nevertheless there remains in the sitter a true power of walking, and in the walker the power of sitting; not indeed in the composed sense as if they could at once walk and stand, but in the divided sense, since any act, although it excludes the opposite act, yet does not exclude the potency to it.
pass_b: So they do grant that the motion of God's grace, the efficacy of his providence too, or even the practical judgment's last dictate, determines a man to act and to will in such a way that the act called free follows necessarily. Once God's grace and providence are at work with their motion and efficacy, the act toward which God prepares, moves and determines the man, whether by the motion of grace or by the efficacy of common providence, cannot fail to be put forth.

But they do not count this as necessity in the proper sense, because a real power not to act coexists with it. When God calls a man according to his purpose, he moves him to believe God and to love God and his neighbour in such a way that faith and love follow infallibly, and with that motion in place the man cannot fail to believe and love. Yet God does not take away his power not to believe and not to love. The act contrary to the divine motion cannot coexist with it, but the power to that contrary act does.

In the same way a seated man must be sitting while he sits and a walking man must be walking while he walks; it is impossible for a seated man not to sit or for a walking man not to walk. Yet the seated man keeps a real power to walk and the walker a real power to sit. This holds not in the composite sense, as if they could walk and stand at once, but in the divided sense, because any act, while it excludes the opposite act, does not exclude the potency for it.

sections.title: So the man moved acts by a necessity of infallibility yet keeps a real power not to act
sections.pass_a: Therefore, according to this doctrine, man efficaciously moved by God to doing this or that, or impelled by the dictate of his own judgment, acts indeed necessarily by a certain necessity of infallibility; but at the same time yet retains a true power of not acting. And he can indeed not act, but yet will certainly act: nor can it happen that the lack of the action should ever be joined with such a judgment, or with a motion of God of that kind.
pass_b: On this teaching, then, a man whom God effectively moves to do this or that, or whom the dictate of his own judgment drives to it, does act necessarily, with a necessity of infallibility, while still keeping a real power not to act.
He is able not to act, yet he will surely act; and the absence of the act can never be found together with such a judgment or with such a motion from God.

sections.title: What the second party means when they say the man so moved cannot not act
sections.pass_a: But those who on the contrary teach that manifold necessity consists with liberty, and that he whom grace moves or the dictate of his own judgment impels to acting, cannot not act, mean nothing else than that it is impossible that a man who is moved by God to some act, by that grace which is said to work in men to will and to perform, or at least by the efficacy of common providence, or also by the judgment of his own reason, should not elicit that act to which he is thus supposed moved and excited: and so that from the positing of such grace and help and also of such a judgment, it necessarily follows that the man will act so, or so.
pass_b: Those on the other side, who teach that necessity of many kinds is compatible with freedom, and that a man moved by grace or driven by his own judgment's dictate to act cannot fail to act, mean only this. When God moves a man to some act, whether by the grace said to work in men both to will and to do, or at least by the efficacy of common providence, or even by the judgment of his own reason, the man cannot fail to produce the act he is assumed to have been moved and stirred to.
So once such grace and help, and such a judgment, are given, it follows necessarily that the man will act in this way or that.

sections.title: They readily grant that the power to the contrary stands with the act itself
sections.pass_a: However they will readily grant, that from him whom grace moves, for example, to praying, and to bestowing alms on a poor man, the power of not praying, and of not bestowing that alms is not at all on that account taken away; nay that with the very act of calling upon God and giving alms the power to the privation of those acts, or also to contrary acts, stands no less, than with the act of speaking stands the power of being silent, and with the act of sitting stands the power of not sitting, or also of walking.
pass_b: Still, they will readily admit that when grace moves someone to pray, say, or to give alms to a poor man, his power not to pray and not to give those alms is not removed on that account.

Indeed, the power to leave those acts undone, or even to do the opposite, coexists with the very act of praying and of giving alms just as much as the power to keep silent coexists with the act of speaking, and the power not to sit, or even to walk, coexists with the act of sitting.

sections.title: Both agree: the act cannot be separated from God's motion, yet a power to cease or to the opposite remains
sections.pass_a: Both therefore agree in this, that it is necessary that he act whom the force and efficacy of divine grace, or of providence, and the dictate of his own reason move and impel to acting, since from that motion of God and determination of his own judgment the action of man cannot be separated: and yet that with an act of that kind, and so with the motion of God to such an act, consists the power to cessation from it, or also to the opposite act, in the manner which has been oftener set forth and repeated.
pass_b: Both sides, then, agree on two points. A man whom the force and efficacy of God's grace or providence, together with his own reason's dictate, moves and drives to act must act, because his action cannot be separated from that motion of God and that determination of his own judgment.
And yet with such an act, and so with God's motion toward it, there coexists a power to stop it or even to do the opposite, in the way that has been explained and repeated more than once.

sections.title: They differ in words but agree in substance
sections.pass_a: Accordingly when these indeed assert that he whom God moves to this, or that act acts necessarily; but others contend that he is impelled to acting by no necessity properly so called, they differ indeed in words, but think the same in fact. Namely the former say that a man of this kind acts necessarily, because it is impossible that his act be separated from the divine motion, which the others do not deny. But according to the latter he is held to acting by no necessity properly so called, because with his very act, and accordingly much more with the motion to the act, there very well consists a power to the contrary act, or at least to the lack of that act, which the former will readily grant.
pass_b: So when one party says that a man whom God moves to a given act acts necessarily, and the other insists that no necessity in the proper sense drives him to act, their words differ but their meaning is the same.

The first party says such a man acts necessarily because his act cannot be separated from God's motion, and the second does not deny it. The second says he is bound to act by no necessity in the proper sense, because a power to the opposite act, or at least to leaving the act undone, sits perfectly well with the act itself and still more with the motion toward it, and the first party readily grants that.

sections.title: The Reformed dispute over indifference can likewise be settled
sections.pass_a: From the same source it appears also that the dissension can easily be composed which still seems to remain among the Doctors of the Reformed School: while some, namely, affirm that liberty of choice includes a certain indifference of the free agent, by which, all things prerequisite to acting being posited, it can act, or not act, do this or that; but others deny that such indifference is included in liberty, or pertains to liberty at all.
pass_b: The same considerations show that the disagreement still apparently left among teachers of the Reformed School can easily be settled.

Some of them hold that freedom of choice includes a certain indifference in the free agent, by which, given everything required beforehand for acting, it can act or not act, and do this or that. Others deny that any such indifference is included in freedom or has anything to do with it.
