sections.title: What the defenders of indifference mean: not equipoise, but a true intrinsic power to act otherwise
sections.pass_a: For those who will have it that liberty is not without some indifference of the free agent, by indifference do not understand that state in which the agent does not incline to one part more than to another, but stands in doubt with equal weight to be impelled hither and thither, which those who think the contrary most of all abhor. For there is not any of those who maintain that indifference, who does not judge that it is found also in him, who by a firm and certain judgment has resolved that this and not another thing must be done by him: and whose will also, by habits deeply rooted, and which he can with the greatest difficulty shake off, is borne most vehemently to this, or that part. And so by the name of indifference, in this business, they designate nothing else than a true and intrinsic potency not only of acting, but also of ceasing from action, not only of doing this, but also something different, or its opposite. Which potency is found not only in him who is doubtful and uncertain whether he should act, or not act, but in him also who in no way hesitates and doubts about that which must or must not be done by him, and who with a fixed and unmoved purpose determines himself to act thus and not otherwise.
pass_b: Those who hold that freedom never exists without some indifference in the free agent do not mean by indifference a state in which the agent leans no more one way than the other and hangs in the balance, equally ready to be pushed either way. That is the very thing their opponents most object to.

None of the defenders of this indifference fails to hold that it is present even in someone who has decided, with firm and sure judgment, that he must do this and nothing else, and whose will is carried with great force in one direction by deep-rooted habits he could shake off only with the utmost difficulty.

In this matter, then, by indifference they mean simply a real, intrinsic power not only to act but also to stop acting, not only to do this but also to do something else or its opposite. That power is found not only in someone who is unsure and torn over whether to act, but also in someone who has no hesitation or doubt about what he should or should not do, and who sets himself, with a fixed and steady purpose, to act in this way and no other.

choices.why: Kept as the Schools' technical term; Le Blanc fixes its sense as a real power to act otherwise, not a state of balance between options.

sections.title: Nor do they mean the act can fail to follow upon efficacious grace and a settled judgment
sections.pass_a: And moreover when they say that a free agent, all things prerequisite to acting being posited, can act or not act, do this, or that, their mind is not that, all things being posited which are prerequired to some act of the will, among which the motion of divine grace has place, and the judgment of the practical mind, the action of the will can fail to follow, and thus the lack of its action be joined with all those things by which the will is moved and disposed to acting. For they confess it impossible that God should move any man by his efficacious grace to some act of piety, and yet that act not be elicited by him: or that someone, all things weighed, should judge that this must be done and desired by him here and now, and yet the same not do and desire it; But they mean only this, that he who, in the manner already stated, is moved to acting, although he will infallibly and certainly act, and it cannot happen that he not act; he, I say, nevertheless retains in himself a true potency of not acting, and of acting otherwise, which remains not only in him who is proximately prepared and disposed to act, but in him himself who already in fact acts; since although with some act its lack, or a contrary act, cannot stand, yet with it the potency to that contrary act can very well be composed, as has already been inculcated many times.
pass_b: Further, when they say that a free agent, given everything required beforehand for acting, can act or not act, and do this or that, they do not mean that the will's act can fail to follow once everything required for some act of will is in place, including the motion of God's grace and the practical judgment of the mind, so that the absence of the act could coexist with everything that moves and disposes the will to act.

They admit it is impossible for God to move someone by his effective grace to an act of godliness and for that act not to be produced, or for someone, having weighed everything, to judge that he must do and seek something here and now and then not do and seek it.

All they mean is this. The man who is moved to act in the way described will act infallibly and surely, and it cannot happen that he does not act; yet he still keeps in himself a real power not to act and to act otherwise. That power remains not only in someone fully prepared and ready to act but in someone actually acting. For although an act cannot coexist with its own absence or with a contrary act, the power to the contrary act can perfectly well coexist with it, as has been stressed many times already.

choices.why: Kept as the Schools' technical term; Le Blanc fixes its sense as a real power to act otherwise, not a state of balance between options.

sections.title: What the deniers of indifference mean: equipoise, in which no Christian theologian ever placed freedom
sections.pass_a: But those who on the contrary contend that some indifference of the agent is not required to liberty of choice, seem by the name of indifference to signify the equipoise (ἰσοῤῥοπία) of the will, when it inclines to this part no more than to another, and is flexible hither no more than thither, in which no one of those who bear the name of Theologian in the Christian Schools, ever placed liberty.
pass_b: Those who argue the other way, that freedom of choice does not require any indifference in the agent, seem to mean by indifference the will's equal balance (ἰσοῤῥοπία), when it leans no more to one side than to the other and can be swayed no more this way than that.
Yet no one who bears the name of theologian in the Christian Schools has ever made freedom consist in that.

choices.why: Kept as the Schools' technical term; Le Blanc fixes its sense as a real power to act otherwise, not a state of balance between options.

sections.title: Nor do they deny the power to act otherwise: neither the act nor grace removes it
sections.pass_a: And likewise when they say it is false that a free agent, all things being posited which are requisite to acting, can act, and not act, do this and that, their opinion is not, that through those things which prepare and impel to acting, the faculty of acting otherwise, or of suspending the action, is taken from the free agent: since they acknowledge that that faculty is not taken away through the act itself; much less through those things which impel to acting. For they do not deny that he who through the grace of God pities the needy, has always in himself the power of not pitying, and that he who despises the pleasures of this world, retains the faculty of seeking and embracing them, which is not taken from him by divine grace. And so they intend nothing else than this, that all things being posited which are required to acting, it cannot happen that a free agent not act: although otherwise there remains in him the faculty by which he could not act, or act otherwise. For example, that it cannot be but that, all things being posited which on God's part are necessary to producing the faith and conversion of a man, the man be converted and believe; although always, and even when he believes and is converted, there remains in him the faculty, by which he could not believe and not be converted.
pass_b: In the same way, when they say it is false that a free agent, given everything required for acting, can act and not act, and do this and that, they do not mean that whatever prepares and drives him to act takes away his ability to act otherwise or to hold the act back. They acknowledge that the act itself does not remove that ability, much less the things that drive him to it.

They do not deny that someone who by God's grace shows mercy to the needy always keeps in himself the power not to show it, or that someone who scorns this world's pleasures keeps the ability to pursue and embrace them; God's grace does not take that ability from him.

Their only point is that once everything required for acting is in place, a free agent cannot fail to act, even though he otherwise keeps an ability by which he could refrain or act differently. For instance, once everything needed on God's side to produce a man's faith and conversion is in place, the man cannot fail to be converted and believe, though always, even while he believes and is converted, he keeps an ability by which he could fail to believe and be converted.

choices.why: Kept as the Schools' technical term; Le Blanc fixes its sense as a real power to act otherwise, not a state of balance between options.

sections.title: So the deniers reject only two things, and the defenders of indifference grant both
sections.pass_a: Whence it is plain that these Theologians, when they deny that liberty consists in a certain indifference of the agent, have only two things before their eyes, of which one is that liberty does not consist in the doubtful state of him who is called free, in which he does not more incline and lean to acting, than to not acting: the other, that, the motion and efficacy of divine grace and providence being posited, and also the dictate of his own judgment, it cannot happen that the free agent not do that to which he is impelled both by that efficacious motion of God, and by his own judgment; both of which those of the Reformed who teach that a certain indifference to acting is included in liberty of choice willingly confess. And Again from what has been said it is no less evident that those Doctors who maintain that indifference have only this in mind, that the divine motion, and the judgment of the practical mind so move man to acting, that on the one part indeed he acts certainly and infallibly, on the other yet the faculty of not acting, or of acting otherwise, is not taken from him. Not otherwise than when man actually acts, the same faculty is not taken from him through the very act to which he has been moved and impelled.
pass_b: This makes it plain that when these theologians deny that freedom consists in some indifference of the agent, they have only two things in view. First, freedom does not consist in a wavering state in which the person called free leans no more toward acting than toward not acting. Second, once God's grace and providence are at work with their motion and efficacy, and the agent's own judgment has given its dictate, the free agent cannot fail to do what God's effective motion and his own judgment drive him to. Both points are readily admitted by those Reformed who teach that freedom of choice includes a certain indifference toward acting.

What has been said shows just as clearly that the teachers who defend that indifference have only this in mind: God's motion and the mind's practical judgment move a man to act in such a way that, on the one hand, he acts surely and infallibly and, on the other, he is not deprived of the ability not to act or to act otherwise. In the same way, when a man actually acts, the act he has been moved and driven to does not take that ability from him.

choices.why: Kept as the Schools' technical term; Le Blanc fixes its sense as a real power to act otherwise, not a state of balance between options.

sections.title: Rightly understood, the Reformed doctrine agrees in substance with the more received Thomists
sections.pass_a: But from all these it is manifest that the doctrine of the Reformed in this part, rightly set forth and understood, and according to the mind of those by whom it is propounded, does not in fact differ from the opinion of those who in the Roman School are called the more received Thomists. For although they contend that liberty is opposed not to compulsion only, but to natural necessity also and necessity properly so called, nevertheless they acknowledge that, all things being posited which are prerequisite to acting, the act of the free creature necessarily follows by a certain necessity of infallibility. Because although a free agent always retains in itself the power of not acting, even when it actually acts, and a fortiori when it is proximate to acting; yet all things being posited which, both on the part of God, and on the part of the intellect, are prerequired that the will may act, it acts certainly and infallibly, and it is impossible that its action not follow. Namely from their doctrine, with all those things which are prerequisite to acting the potency of not acting, or of acting otherwise, can very well be joined and consist, yet not the lack of the act, and much less the contrary act.
pass_b: From all this it is clear that the Reformed teaching on this point, correctly stated and understood as its own exponents intend it, does not in fact differ from the view of those in the Roman School called the more widely received Thomists.

These Thomists maintain that freedom is opposed not only to compulsion but also to natural necessity, necessity in the proper sense. Even so, they recognize that once everything required for acting is in place, the free creature's act follows necessarily, with a necessity of infallibility.

A free agent always keeps in itself the power not to act, even while it is actually acting, and all the more when it is on the point of acting. But once everything required on God's side and on the intellect's side for the will to act is in place, the will acts surely and infallibly, and its action cannot fail to follow. On their teaching, then, the power not to act or to act otherwise can perfectly well coexist with everything required for acting, but the absence of the act cannot, and still less a contrary act.

choices.why: Kept as the technical phrase both Reformed parties use; it marks the necessity that removes the power to act otherwise, as against a necessity of infallibility.

sections.title: Their indifference is only the true power not to act, as Alvarez states (De auxiliis IV.14)
sections.pass_a: And so by the indifference to acting, or not acting, in which according to their mind liberty is to be placed, or which at least is necessarily joined to liberty, they understand no other, than that which has already been described above. To wit neither such by which a free cause may be conceived doubtful and uncertain whether it should act, or not act; nor yet by which, all things being posited which are requisite to acting, it may happen that a free agent as much not act, as act; but which is nothing else than a true power of not acting, and of acting otherwise, which remains in a free cause when, all things being posited which are required to acting, it not only is proximate to acting, but also will infallibly and certainly act, as Alvarez very clearly and expressly sets forth his opinion on this matter in the sum of the work on the helps of divine grace book 4. chap. 14. whence have been taken the words which were related by us from the same Alvarez in the former disputation.
pass_b: By the indifference to acting or not acting in which, on their view, freedom must be placed, or which at least necessarily goes with freedom, they mean nothing other than what was described above.

It is not an indifference that would picture a free cause as unsure and torn over whether to act, nor one by which, given everything required for acting, the free agent might just as well not act as act. It is simply a real power not to act and to act otherwise. That power remains in a free cause when, with everything required for acting in place, it is not only on the point of acting but will act infallibly and surely.

Alvarez sets out his view on this very clearly and explicitly in the summary of his work on the helps of divine grace, book 4, chapter 14, the source of the words of his that we quoted in the preceding disputation.

lemmas.gloss: in the sum of the work on the helps of divine grace

sections.title: Rivet's account of free choice is taken word for word from Alvarez
sections.pass_a: And indeed that the opinion of that Diego Alvarez, and of others who with him are called the more recent Thomists, is here plainly the same with the opinion of the Doctors of the Reformed Church, a fit witness is that most Learned Man Andrew Rivet some years ago Professor in the University of Leiden, while he would express his mind on the liberty of human choice in no other words than those which are taken from Alvarez himself. In the sum of controversies tract. 4. quest. 3. For he confesses that the definition of free choice can be tolerated by which it is called a faculty of the will by which, all things prerequisite to acting being posited, it can act, or not act, provided this be understood not in the composed sense, but in the divided sense, Namely, he says, if one say that all things antecedently requisite, according to the order of reason, or of time to the act, being posited, free choice can operate, or not operate, so, to wit, that with the same prerequisites there stand at once in free choice the faculty and potency, by which it could operate, or not operate if it would, as Diego Alvarez distinguishes, because even the efficacious motion of God by which the will is determined to such an act, does not take from free choice the faculty of operating that act or of operating the contrary act, but only effects, that while free choice can operate or not operate such an act infallibly, yet it operates it freely. Which when it does, the potency to another remains, because to such acts it is not naturally determined. For as the same says, in a contingent and free cause, there is at once a potency to either opposite, yet there is not a potency to opposites to be had at once, because the potency to one act, is not repugnant to the potency to the contrary act, nor is it repugnant even to the contrary act, but contrary acts are repugnant among themselves in the same subject; whence created free choice not only before it is determined to one act, but also in the very instant, in which it is determined by God, and determines itself to the same act, has at once a potency by which it can produce the contrary act if it will, yet not to having the contrary act at the same time, because two contrary acts cannot be at once in the same potency, but successively. All which words have been either expressly cited, or at least borrowed from Diego Alvarez, as also that which he subjoins as the conclusion of the same doctor which is approved by him, namely, that it is not of the nature of free choice or of its definition, that, all things being posited antecedently prerequisite according to the order of causality to operating such an act, it can not operate the same act in the composed sense, if the composition be made between such prerequisites, and the lack of such an act, or the contrary act, that is, that with the efficacious help of God, it does not stand at once that free choice not produce the act of love, or elicit an act contrary to the love of God.
pass_b: That the view of this Diego Alvarez, and of the others called with him the more recent Thomists, is here exactly the same as that of the teachers of the Reformed Church is well attested by the very learned Andrew Rivet, some years ago professor at the University of Leiden. When he set out his own mind on the freedom of human choice, he used no words but those taken from Alvarez himself, in his Summa of controversies, treatise 4, question 3.

He grants that one may accept the definition of free choice as 'a faculty of the will by which, given everything required beforehand for acting, it can act or not act', provided this is taken in the divided sense, not the composite. 'That is,' he says, 'if someone says that, given everything required beforehand for the act in the order of reason or of time, free choice can act or not act, meaning that together with those same prerequisites there is in free choice the ability and power by which it could act or not act if it wished, as Diego Alvarez distinguishes. For even God's effective motion, by which the will is determined to such an act, does not take from free choice the ability to perform that act or the contrary one; it only brings it about that, while free choice is able to perform such an act or not, it performs it infallibly and yet freely. When it does so, the power to another act remains, because it is not determined by nature to such acts.

For, as the same author says, in a contingent and free cause there is at once a power to either of two opposites, but not a power to have the opposites at once. A power to one act does not conflict with a power to the contrary act, nor even with the contrary act itself, though contrary acts do conflict with each other in the same subject. Hence created free choice, not only before it is determined to one act but in the very instant in which God determines it and it determines itself to that act, has at the same moment a power by which it can produce the contrary act if it wishes. It has no power to have the contrary act at the same moment, because two contrary acts cannot be in the same power at once, only one after the other.'

All these words are either quoted outright or at least borrowed from Diego Alvarez. So is what Rivet adds as that teacher's conclusion, which he endorses: that it does not belong to the nature or definition of free choice that, given everything required beforehand in the order of causality for performing such an act, it can leave that same act undone in the composite sense, if the composition is made between those prerequisites and the absence of the act or a contrary act. In other words, with God's effective help it cannot at the same time be true that free choice does not produce the act of love, or that it produces an act contrary to the love of God.

according to the order of causality

sections.title: The only real controversy left to the Reformed is with the Molinists
sections.pass_a: Therefore there remains to the Reformed no controversy, which is real and of any moment, except with those who in the Roman School are called Molinists, the denomination being taken from Luis Molina a most celebrated Jesuit, who wrote and taught about a hundred years ago. For the indifference to acting and not acting, in which liberty of choice consists, and the common definition by which it is said to be that by which, all things prerequisite to acting being posited, the will can act and not act, do this or that, they understand far otherwise than the more recent Thomists, as we made manifest in the preceding disputation.
pass_b: So no dispute of substance or of any weight is left for the Reformed except with those in the Roman School called Molinists, after the famous Jesuit Luis de Molina, who wrote and taught about a century ago.

They understand the indifference to acting and not acting in which freedom of choice consists, and the familiar definition that calls it 'that by which, given everything required beforehand for acting, the will can act and not act, do this or that', very differently from the more recent Thomists, as we showed in the preceding disputation.

sections.title: What the Molinists grant: not equipoise; habits; the composite sense; not a power of good and evil
sections.pass_a: They confess indeed with others that by the indifference about which the question is here, is not signified that constitution of the will by which it inclines no more hither than thither, but hangs between two opposites, as if suspended in equilibrium: since they acknowledge that nothing is prejudiced to liberty by habits by which the will is strongly inclined to doing this rather than that, and can with difficulty be borne elsewhere. And moreover they do not deny that in a certain composed sense it is false that the will can act and not act, do this and that; namely, if anyone think that by this is signified that the act and its lack, or two contrary acts can stand and be composed in the will at once. They admit also that by the indifference in which the essence of liberty consists, is not understood the power of acting well or ill. For they acknowledge that liberty of choice remains even in him who cannot act well, as in the damned spirits: and much more still that it is found in him who cannot act ill, as in the saints who see the face of God, and reign with him in heaven.
pass_b: They do agree with the others that the indifference in question here does not mean a condition of the will in which it leans no more one way than the other and hangs between two opposites as if balanced on scales. They grant that freedom suffers nothing from habits that strongly incline the will to do this rather than that and make it hard for it to go another way.

Nor do they deny that, in a certain composite sense, it is false that the will can act and not act, or do this and that, namely if someone takes this to mean that an act and its absence, or two contrary acts, can be present and combined in the will at once.

They also accept that the indifference in which the essence of freedom consists is not the power to act well or badly. They acknowledge that freedom of choice remains even in one who cannot act well, as in the damned spirits, and is present still more in one who cannot act badly, as in the saints who see God's face and reign with him in heaven.

sections.title: What the Molinists defend: the act may fail to follow upon all prerequisites; Reformed and recent Thomists deny it
sections.pass_a: But they sharply defend that the will is in itself so undetermined and indifferent, that all things prerequisite to acting being posited, whether on the part of God, or on the part of the object, or on the part of the intellect, it can happen and often also does happen, that the will does not act: and so that there is nothing of those things which antecedently move and incite the will to acting, which being posited the action of the will cannot fail to follow, and often also in fact does not follow: and thus with all those things which precede the action of the will, and are prerequired to it, there can really be joined and composed, not only the power to not acting or doing something else, but the very lack of the act, and also the contrary act. Which is denied, as is sufficiently clear from the foregoing, not only by the Reformed, but also by those more recent Thomists. Indeed they think that with those things which either on the part of God, or on the part of the intellect are necessary to acting, there can indeed consist in the will the power of not acting, or of doing the opposite; but yet that these being posited the will always acts, nor can it happen that it fall out otherwise: since from this hypothesis the will acts certainly and infallibly, although it retain in itself the potency of not acting.
pass_b: What they do defend, and strongly, is that the will is in itself so undetermined and indifferent that, given everything required beforehand for acting, whether on God's side, the object's, or the intellect's, the will can fail to act, and often actually does. Nothing, then, that moves and stirs the will to act beforehand is such that, once it is in place, the will's act cannot fail to follow; quite often it really does not follow.

So everything that precedes the will's act and is required for it can really be combined not only with a power not to act or to do something else but with the very absence of the act, and even with the contrary act.

As the foregoing shows clearly enough, both the Reformed and those more recent Thomists deny this. They hold that a power not to act, or to do the opposite, can indeed coexist in the will with what God's side or the intellect's side requires for acting, but that once those are in place the will always acts and nothing else can happen. On that supposition the will acts surely and infallibly, though it keeps in itself the power not to act.

sections.title: Rome has not defined the dispute; Paul V and Clement VIII seemed to favour the Thomists, Innocent X and Alexander VII the other side
sections.pass_a: Further although that dispute has often been moved and agitated before the Roman Pontiffs, and a body of Cardinals deputed for this, yet hitherto they have not yet defined it, and have willed it to be lawful for their people to hold and defend this or that opinion at their choice. Although as about the beginning of this century and the end of the preceding the Roman Pontiffs Paul V. and Clement VIII. seemed to favour the opinion of the Thomists. So in these last years their successors Innocent X. and Alexander VII. seem to have favoured the opposite doctrine more. Whence it has come about that it has now become far more common in the Roman School, and is held by the greatest part of the Theologians.
pass_b: The dispute has often been raised and argued before the popes of Rome and before a body of cardinals appointed for the purpose, yet so far they have not settled it, and they have allowed their people to hold and defend either view as they choose.

Around the turn of this century, at the close of the last, Popes Paul V and Clement VIII seemed to favour the Thomists' view. In these last years their successors Innocent X and Alexander VII seem to have leaned rather toward the opposite teaching. As a result it has now become by far the more common view in the Roman School and is held by most of its theologians.

sections.title: Alignment: Jansenists and recent Thomists with the Dort Reformed; Remonstrants with the Molinists
sections.pass_a: And moreover as in this part some Doctors of the Roman Church, as those who are called Jansenists, and those more recent Thomists also, attack the Molinists with common arms with those Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort: so on the side of the Molinists stand, and most sharply defend their doctrine in this question, those of the Reformed who in the Netherlands are called Remonstrants or Arminians, and others who do not follow the Synod of Dort.
pass_b: On this point, moreover, some teachers of the Roman Church, namely the so-called Jansenists and those more recent Thomists as well, join forces against the Molinists with the Reformed who subscribe to the Synod of Dort.

On the Molinists' side, by contrast, stand those Reformed in the Netherlands called Remonstrants or Arminians, along with others who do not follow the Synod of Dort, and they defend the Molinist teaching on this question very vigorously.

sections.title: First Reformed objection: the Molinist view lessens the efficacy of grace (1 Corinthians 4:7)
sections.pass_a: But their opinion is rejected by the Doctors of the Reformed School chiefly on this account that it diminishes the efficacy of divine grace, and attributes more to free choice than is right in the business of salvation. For, scripture teaching, whatever good is in us, must be credited wholly to divine grace; according to that of the Apostle, What do you have that you did not receive? but from that doctrine it follows, that a man can believe and love God, is indeed to be attributed to the helps of grace, moving and exciting man to faith and love, but that man consents to grace moving him and determines himself to believing and loving God, so depends on liberty of choice that it is not properly an effect of divine grace, since grace being posited that consent often does not follow; and thus divine grace can be called only its condition, or cause without which not.
pass_b: The Reformed teachers reject their view mainly because it lessens the efficacy of God's grace and gives free choice more than its due in the matter of salvation.

Scripture teaches that every good thing in us must be credited entirely to God's grace, as the Apostle says: 'What do you have that you did not receive?' On this teaching, however, the fact that a man is able to believe and love God is indeed owed to the helps of grace, which move and stir him to faith and love. But the fact that he consents to the grace that moves him and settles himself to believe and love God depends so much on his freedom of choice that it is not, properly, an effect of God's grace, since the consent often fails to follow when grace is given. God's grace could then be called only a condition of it, a cause without which it would not happen.

sections.title: Second objection: the will, not grace, would distinguish believers from unbelievers
sections.pass_a: Moreover scripture teaches that it is divine grace which puts the distinction among men, between those namely who are converted and who are not converted, between believers and unbelievers between those who obey God calling and those who resist him: according to that of Paul, Who distinguishes you? but from the doctrine of those of whom we now treat, it follows that not divine grace; but simply the human will establishes this distinction among men. For it supposes, equal grace being offered to several, this one to believe; that one not to believe; this one to be converted, that one not to be converted: And consequently that this one rather than that believes and is converted, ought not to be referred to any efficacy of grace, but only to the free determination of the human will; because namely this one willed to consent to grace moving and prevenient, but that one would not.
pass_b: Scripture also teaches that it is God's grace that sets people apart from one another: those who are converted from those who are not, believers from unbelievers, those who obey God's call from those who resist it. As Paul says, 'Who makes you different?'

The doctrine we are now examining, however, implies that the difference between people is made not by God's grace but simply by the human will. It assumes that when equal grace is offered to several people, one believes and another does not, one is converted and another is not.

It follows that one person's believing and being converted rather than another's must be traced not to any efficacy of grace but only to the free self-determination of the human will, because this one chose to consent to the grace that moved him and came first to him, while that one refused.

sections.title: Third objection: grace would give only the powers, not the willing and doing (Philippians 2:13)
sections.pass_a: Add that if divine grace only so moves, prepares and incites men to willing and performing those things which God commands, that yet the very willing and performing, it being posited, can fail to follow in man, and in fact often does not follow, it works indeed in man the powers or dispositions necessary to willing and performing good, but not the very willing and performing. But the Apostle on the contrary testifies, That it is God who works in us both to will and to perform according to his good will. Phil. 2. 13.
pass_b: Moreover, if God's grace merely moves, prepares and stirs people to will and to carry out what he commands, in such a way that the willing and doing themselves can fail to follow in a person once grace is given, and in fact often do fail, then grace produces in a person the strength or the dispositions needed for willing and doing good, but not the willing and doing themselves.
The Apostle testifies the opposite: it is God who works in us both to will and to do for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13).

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.

sections.title: Fourth objection: Christ teaches a grace that brings all who receive it to him (John 6:45)
sections.pass_a: Lastly if, all things prerequisite to acting being posited, even on the part of God, not excluding any efficacy of grace, it can always happen that the will does not act, there is given no grace of God, at least ordinary, which the conversion of man follows infallibly and certainly, and by which all who are gifted, none excepted, come to Christ. But on the contrary Christ himself teaches that there is a certain grace of God, which no one receives who does not come to him. For whoever, he says, has heard and learned from the Father comes to me. John chapter six.
pass_b: Finally, if the will can always fail to act even when everything required for acting is in place, on God's side too and with no efficacy of grace whatever left out, then there is no grace of God, at least no ordinary grace, that a person's conversion follows infallibly and surely, and that brings everyone who receives it, without exception, to Christ.
Christ himself teaches the opposite: there is a grace of God that no one receives without coming to him. 'Everyone,' he says, 'who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me' (John 6).

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.

sections.title: Christ's argument in John 6:43-45 would fail if many who are drawn do not believe
sections.pass_a: And certainly if many of those who are drawn by the Father's grace and are inwardly taught by God, yet do not believe in Christ, nor come to him, how would Christ in the same place bring this reason why not all who hear the Gospel come to him; namely, that it is necessary that those who come to him be drawn and taught by the Father? Murmur not, he says, among yourselves. No one can come to me, unless the Father who sent me draw him. It is written in the Prophets, And they shall all be taught of God. Every one therefore who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me. Assuredly if those very ones who do not believe the Gospel are drawn by the Father's grace, it would be absurd to say, Do not wonder that these and those to whom the Gospel was preached have yet not believed in the Gospel; since it is necessary that those who believe in the Gospel be drawn by divine grace.
pass_b: Surely, if many of those whom the Father's grace draws and God teaches inwardly still do not believe in Christ or come to him, how could Christ give, in that same passage, this as the reason why not everyone who hears the gospel comes to him, namely that those who come to him must be drawn and taught by the Father?

'Do not grumble among yourselves,' he says. 'No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. It is written in the Prophets: And they will all be taught by God. Everyone, then, who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me.'

If the very people who do not believe the gospel are drawn by the Father's grace, it would make no sense to say: 'Do not be surprised that this person and that, to whom the gospel was preached, have still not believed it, since those who believe the gospel must be drawn by God's grace.'

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.

sections.title: Conclusion: freedom is wrongly placed in a power not to act even in the composite sense
sections.pass_a: Since therefore there is a certain divine grace, and indeed common to all the elect, upon whose motion and impulse the conversion of man follows infallibly and certainly; and yet by the consent of all the conversion of man to God is a free act of the will: it is plain that liberty is ill placed in this, that, all things prerequisite to acting being posited and the ordinary motion of grace itself, the will can always as well not act as act, not only in the divided sense but in the composed sense also, so that with that motion of grace there can be joined the lack of the act to which it moves man.
pass_b: There is, then, a divine grace, shared indeed by all the elect, whose motion and impulse a person's conversion follows infallibly and surely; and yet everyone agrees that a person's conversion to God is a free act of the will.

It is clear, therefore, that freedom is wrongly located in the will's always being able, with everything required for acting in place, including grace's ordinary motion, as much not to act as to act, and that not only in the divided sense but also in the composite sense, so that grace's motion could coexist with the absence of the act toward which it moves a person.

sections.title: Safer definitions of free choice: those of Alvarez and of Bellarmine
sections.pass_a: Therefore than that common description of Free Choice by which it is defined a faculty by which, all things prerequisite to acting being posited, one can act and not act, do this or that, safer is that which Alvarez substituted, Free choice is a faculty of the will and of reason to acting or not acting whichever one pleases and to doing one or the other. Or also that of Bellarmine, Free choice is a free power of choosing, out of those things which conduce to some end, one before another, or of rejecting or accepting one and the same thing at our choice, attributed or granted for the great glory of God.
pass_b: So, rather than the familiar description of free choice as 'a faculty by which, given everything required beforehand for acting, a person can act and not act, do this or that', it is safer to use the one Alvarez put in its place: 'Free choice is a faculty of will and reason for acting or not acting, as one pleases, and for doing one thing or the other.'

Or else Bellarmine's: 'Free choice is a free power, given or granted for the great glory of God, to choose one thing over another among the things that lead to some end, or to reject or accept one and the same thing as we decide.'
